title: SMTP-DANE (RFC 7672): dedicated entry point, not a reuse of the HTTPS DANE path
description:
## Why

RFC 7672 SMTP-DANE has the strongest production deployment of any DANE flavour — MTAs negotiating TLS routinely use it for trust. A workspace that adopts DANE for HTTPS and not SMTP is incomplete. Replaces PKIX-j32w.6, which asked the question against a function (verify_smtp_signer) that does not exist and would have been the wrong home anyway: SMTP-DANE validates a mail SERVER's TLS certificate, not a signer.

## Why this cannot reuse verify_tls_server's DANE path

Three behavioural differences from HTTPS-DANE. The first makes a shared path wrong rather than merely incomplete.

### 1. Usage filtering — CONFIRM THIS FIRST

Current understanding is that RFC 7672 requires SMTP clients to ignore PKIX-TA(0) and PKIX-EE(1) records outright, because public CA trust is not meaningful between MTAs with no user to see a warning: only DANE-TA(2) and DANE-EE(3) apply.

THIS IS NOT CONFIRMED. Read RFC 7672 §3.1 and the surrounding text before writing any code. If it holds, then a shared code path with verify_tls_server would honour usage-0 and usage-1 records that SMTP-DANE requires be ignored — a silent policy violation, and the reason this needs its own entry point. If it does not hold, re-evaluate whether a shared path with a mode flag is adequate after all.

### 2. DNSSEC-validated MX lookup — reaches into the resolver

The TLSA owner name derives from an MX lookup, and that lookup must itself be DNSSEC-validated. An unvalidated MX lookup lets an attacker rewrite the MX record and point the connection at a server whose TLSA record they also control, which defeats the whole mechanism.

This is a pkix-dane-resolver requirement, not a wrapper concern: it needs a validated multi-step lookup (MX, then TLSA under the resulting hostname), with the DNSSEC status of BOTH steps surfaced. pkix-dane's TlsaResolver trait as shipped resolves a single TlsaName and has no MX concept. Expect either an additional trait method or a sibling trait in pkix-dane-resolver. Check whether this changes what PKIX-j32w.2 should build before that bead starts.

### 3. Reference identity

Which name the certificate must match follows RFC 7672's MX-derived rules rather than RFC 6125 hostname matching. Determine how this composes with pkix-identity rather than reimplementing name matching.

## Placement — open

PKIX-j32w.6 left this open: pkix-chain wrapper, or a sibling pkix-smtp crate. Decide once the resolver-side shape from difference 2 is known, since an MX-aware resolver trait may make a sibling crate the natural home.

## Also in scope

- RFC 7672's own opportunistic-vs-mandatory posture at the SMTP level, and how it composes with the DaneFailurePolicy decided in PKIX-j32w.4. These are different layers and may not agree; work out which wins.
- Whether the dane / dane-resolver feature split decided on PKIX-j32w.3 extends here unchanged.

## Depends on

pkix-dane 0.2.0 (shipped). Resolver work is PKIX-j32w.2; this bead should be read before that one starts, because difference 2 may widen its scope.

## Acceptance

[ ] RFC 7672 usage-filtering requirement confirmed against the RFC text and recorded
[ ] MX lookup is DNSSEC-validated, with the status of both lookup steps surfaced to the caller
[ ] Usage 0 and 1 records handled per the confirmed RFC requirement
[ ] Reference identity follows RFC 7672, composed with pkix-identity rather than reimplemented
[ ] Placement decided and recorded
notes:
PIECES A, B AND C DONE 2026-11-24. The SMTP DANE path is complete through verification. Only the async resolver driver remains.

## What exists

A. pkix_identity::verify_dns_name_with_cn_fallback -- RFC 7672 section 3.2.3 matching (14 tests)
B. pkix_dane::smtp -- SmtpIdentities (the section 3.2.2 identifier set), verify_smtp_name (18 tests)
C. pkix_dane::smtp_lookup -- MxResolution sans-IO discovery state machine (27 tests)
D. pkix_chain::verify_smtp_server_dane -- the entry point (11 tests)

Behind the `smtp` feature on pkix-dane, pulled in by pkix-chain's `dane` feature. Builds for thumbv7em-none-eabi. 2028 workspace tests pass.

## THE FAILURE-POLICY QUESTION, RESOLVED DIFFERENTLY THAN FILED

This bead expected to reconcile section 3.2's MUST NOT with DaneFailurePolicy, probably by offering an SMTP function that takes no policy so it CANNOT fall back.

Mark redirected it: messages should still be deliverable when DANE fails, we just need to know it failed so they can be tagged, routed, or processed.

That is the better design and it dissolves the problem rather than solving it. The function REPORTS; it does not decide. Every outcome is Ok, including authentication failure, and there is no policy parameter at all -- not because fallback is forbidden, but because the verdict is an input to the MTA's decision rather than a substitute for it. An MTA cannot tag or route on a DANE failure that arrives indistinguishable from a malformed call.

So:
- SmtpDaneVerdict::{Authenticated, NotApplicable, Failed}, all Ok
- rfc7672_permits_delivery() is section 3.2's MUST NOT as a predicate, false only for Failed -- a conforming MTA is one line away, a non-conforming one has to visibly ignore it
- is_authenticated() is the narrower question, because a log claiming a secure channel needs that one and not the first
- SmtpDaneFailure separates four operational problems, since an MTA reporting to a postmaster wants to say which

The rustdoc states the REASON behind the MUST NOT rather than just citing it: a failure where usable secure records exist means either the server is misconfigured or the connection is intercepted, and the sender cannot tell which. It also records that delivering-with-the-failure-logged is coherent for deployments the RFC was not written for, such as a staged rollout measuring DANE before enforcing it in the manner of DMARC p=none.

Keeping NotApplicable and Failed apart is the point of the type. Collapsing them would let a log claim an authenticated channel for a cleartext delivery, or read active interception as a quiet absence of DANE.

## Section 6 was incomplete and is now fixed

Reading section 6 before the entry point, as this bead required, found a real gap: "With mandatory DANE TLS, when no usable TLSA records are found, message delivery is delayed." `mandatory` was being enforced only at the MX step, so a server that published nothing usable was still offered for UNAUTHENTICATED delivery -- defeating the policy it was set for.

Fixed: a host without usable records is passed over, the next in preference order is tried, and delivery is delayed only when none has any. New DelayReason::MandatoryDaneWithoutUsableTlsa, distinct from MandatoryDaneWithInsecureMx because the remedies differ -- the first is the receiving domain's TLSA records, the second its DNSSEC.

First attempt at this was wrong in two ways worth remembering: it delayed on the FIRST host without records rather than trying the next, and the "skipped for want of TLSA" flag survived a later host succeeding. Both caught by tests.

## No trust-store parameter, which was a late simplification

DANE-EE(3) validates no path. DANE-TA(2) validates to the anchor its own record supplies and to that anchor ALONE -- merging it with a caller's store would implement "DANE-TA or any CA", weaker than either, and pkix-chain's existing dane.rs already had that right with a comment saying so. PKIX-TA(0) and PKIX-EE(1), the two usages that would consult a store, are unusable here per section 3.1.3.

So no code path reads caller anchors, and the signature stopped accepting them. The first draft merged the DANE anchor into the caller's anchors, which would have been the exact weakening dane.rs warns about.

## FINDING: a Web PKI profile silently breaks SMTP DANE

BasicTlsProfile sets require_subject_alt_name. Correct for the Web PKI; wrong here, because section 3.2.3 consults the commonName precisely for MTA certificates that carry their name only there. Such a certificate is rejected during PATH VALIDATION, before any name check runs, reporting PathValidationFailed(Path(MissingSan)) -- which gives a debugger no reason to suspect the profile.

Documented on verify_smtp_server_dane. Filed separately for a shipped SMTP profile, since documentation does not help someone who reaches for the obvious profile and never reads the warning.

Affects DANE-TA(2) only; DANE-EE(3) validates no path.

## Testing notes

The DANE-TA SUCCESS path is tested, not only its failures. Without it, an implementation that could never authenticate via usage 2 would have passed every other DANE-TA assertion in the file -- all of which were failure cases, because the PKITS fixtures carry no usable SAN.

One test expectation was wrong and is corrected with its reasoning in a comment: a DANE-TA record need not name a certificate the peer sent, since RFC 7671 lets it designate an anchor by digest alone. So an unrelated anchor is honoured and then fails PATH BUILDING rather than failing to match -- and the resulting verdict is the more useful one.

The MX-preference MUST was mutation-tested: reversing the sort fails that test and two others.

## What remains

The async driver in pkix-dane-resolver: MX, A/AAAA and TLSA lookups feeding MxResolution::absorb. Mechanical now the policy is settled -- hickory wiring plus Proof-to-DnssecStatus, which HickoryTlsaResolver::proof_to_status already does. Note the section 2.2.2 ordering requirement is enforced by the state machine, so the driver only has to answer what it is asked for.

## Not read

RFC 7671 section 5.2 (bears on DANE-TA date and name checks; flagged on the profile bead), RFC 7672 sections 2.1.2 and 2.1.3 in full, section 8.1 (SNI).

## Acceptance

[x] Usage-filtering requirement confirmed -- undefined/MAY, not MUST
[x] CN-ID decided: opt-in function on pkix-identity
[x] Reference identifier set per 3.2.2, matching per 3.2.3
[x] Placement decided
[x] Sections 2.1 and 2.2 read before designing the MX lookup
[x] MX lookup with both DNSSEC statuses surfaced, honouring the MX-preference and A/AAAA-before-TLSA MUSTs
[x] Section 3.2 reconciled -- by reporting rather than by policy, per Mark's redirection
[x] Section 6 read, and the gap it exposed fixed
[x] The entry point
[ ] The async driver in pkix-dane-resolver
close_reason:
FIXED 2026-11-24. RFC 7672 SMTP DANE is implemented end to end: identity matching, discovery, verification, and the async driver.

## What shipped

| Piece | Where | Tests |
|---|---|---|
| section 3.2.3 matching, with CN-ID fallback | pkix_identity::verify_dns_name_with_cn_fallback | 14 |
| section 3.2.2 identifier set + usage gate | pkix_dane::smtp | 18 |
| sections 2.1/2.2/6 discovery state machine | pkix_dane::smtp_lookup | 30 |
| the entry point | pkix_chain::verify_smtp_server_dane | 11 |
| async driver | pkix_dane_resolver::SmtpDiscovery | 9 |

Behind pkix-dane's `smtp` feature, pulled in by pkix-chain's `dane` feature. Builds for thumbv7em-none-eabi. 2040 workspace tests pass.

Verified live against zones nobody here controls, with PKIX_DANE_RESOLVER=9.9.9.9: freebsd.org yields mx1.freebsd.org with one usable DANE-EE record and mx_secure=true, exercising MX lookup, address lookup, TLSA lookup and DNSSEC validation against IANA's anchors in one pass.

## The bead's central premise was wrong, and checking it first was the right call

This bead claimed RFC 7672 REQUIRES SMTP clients to ignore PKIX-TA(0) and PKIX-EE(1), making a shared code path with the HTTPS entry point a policy violation. Section 3.1.3 says servers SHOULD NOT publish them for port 25 and leaves client treatment UNDEFINED, with a MAY to treat them as unusable. Honouring them would have been permitted.

The separate entry point was still right, but on the other two differences -- the identifier set and the DNSSEC-validated MX lookup. The implementation documents that it TAKES the MAY rather than claiming conformance it does not have.

## The failure-policy question was resolved differently than filed

The plan was an SMTP function taking no failure policy so it COULD NOT fall back after a DANE failure. Mark redirected: messages should stay deliverable, we just need to know DANE failed so they can be tagged, routed or processed.

That is better and it dissolves the problem. The function REPORTS; it does not decide. All three outcomes are Ok, including failure, and there is no policy parameter -- not because fallback is forbidden but because the verdict is an input to the MTA's decision. An MTA cannot tag or route on a failure indistinguishable from a malformed call.

rfc7672_permits_delivery() carries section 3.2's MUST NOT as a predicate, so a conforming MTA is one line away and a non-conforming one visibly ignores it. is_authenticated() is the narrower question, because NotApplicable also permits delivery and a log claiming a secure channel needs the second.

## Decisions, with reasons

CN-ID went to pkix-identity as a separately-named opt-in function, not an SMTP-specific matcher, so the workspace keeps exactly ONE wildcard implementation -- a second would be a divergence hazard and wildcard bugs are security bugs. Also AGENTS.md #5: declining to implement a standards-track IETF requirement anywhere would have been this workspace making policy.

Sans-IO for discovery, which cost less than expected. The decisions are pure functions of DNS answers, so the two surprising MUSTs are testable by scripting answers rather than standing up a resolver, and the async driver became a thin loop that cannot get the ordering wrong because it only answers what it is asked.

No trust-store parameter on the entry point. DANE-EE validates no path; DANE-TA validates to its own record's anchor ALONE, since merging would implement "DANE-TA or any CA"; and the two usages that would consult a store are unusable here. The first draft merged them, which pkix-chain's existing dane.rs already warns against in a comment.

## The two MUSTs a naive implementation violates

MX PREFERENCE OUTRANKS CHANNEL SECURITY (2.2.1). A worse-preference host with TLSA records must not preempt a better-preference host without them. Preferring the DANE-capable host is a conformance bug and the obvious thing to write. Mutation-tested: reversing the sort fails that test and two others.

ADDRESS LOOKUPS PRECEDE TLSA LOOKUPS (2.2.2), and with an insecure address answer no TLSA query is issued AT ALL. That is the half that protects against load-balancing nameservers at large providers which answer TLSA with SERVFAIL instead of an insecure negative reply -- a query never sent cannot strand a message.

## Gaps found by reading rather than by guessing

Reading section 6 before the entry point, as this bead required, found that `mandatory` was enforced only at the MX step -- so a server publishing nothing usable was still offered for UNAUTHENTICATED delivery, defeating the policy it was set for. Now the host is passed over, the next tried, and delivery delayed only when none has usable records.

Reading section 2.1.1 found that "indeterminate" folds into "insecure" for this profile. Collapsed at the boundary in RrsetTrust so no decision site has to remember.

Section 2.2.1's "the MX RRset (or any CNAME leading to it)" means an insecure CNAME taints an otherwise-signed MX RRset. A last-answer-wins implementation misses it; the machine only ever weakens mx_secure.

## Gap found by live testing, which a synthetic fixture would not have caught

huque.com publishes PKIX-EE(1) ALONGSIDE DANE-EE(3). TlsaRecord::is_usable asks whether a record parses and carries an assigned usage, not whether this profile can authenticate with it -- so usage-0 and usage-1 records survived discovery's filter and made dane_records() report Some, claiming DANE applied when nothing present could authenticate, and under mandatory policy offering such a host instead of delaying.

Fixed: dane_records() and identities() require a DANE-EE or DANE-TA record. The records are still CARRIED in tlsa_response(), deliberately, because the entry point needs them to report "published only PKIX usages" distinctly from "published nothing" -- a misconfiguration worth telling a postmaster about.

Worth noting as a method: the live test found this by failing on a wrong assumption about a real zone. A synthetic PKIX-only fixture would have tested the filter and missed the mixed case entirely.

## Filed separately

- An SMTP profile for pkix-profiles. BasicTlsProfile sets require_subject_alt_name, correct for the Web PKI and wrong here, so it rejects the CN-only certificates section 3.2.3 exists to accommodate -- during PATH VALIDATION, reporting PathValidationFailed(MissingSan), which points nowhere near the profile. Documented on the function, but documentation does not help someone who reaches for the obvious profile.
- debian.org's TLSA RRset returning Indeterminate under hickory despite a DS record and an AD-setting upstream, while three other signed zones validate Secure through the same resolver. Pre-existing; resolve() reports the same.

## Not read

RFC 7671 section 5.2 (bears on DANE-TA date and name checks; noted on the profile bead), RFC 7672 sections 2.1.2 and 2.1.3 in full, section 8.1 (SNI).

## Acceptance

[x] Usage-filtering requirement confirmed against the RFC text -- undefined/MAY, not MUST, and this bead's claim was wrong
[x] CN-ID decided: opt-in function on pkix-identity
[x] Reference identifier set per 3.2.2, matching per 3.2.3
[x] Placement decided and recorded
[x] Sections 2.1, 2.2 and 6 read before the code that depends on them
[x] MX lookup DNSSEC-validated with both steps' statuses surfaced, honouring both MUSTs
[x] Section 3.2 reconciled -- by reporting rather than by policy
[x] The entry point
[x] The async driver, verified live
